title: Supervision 4 short-answer questions
description: Three short-answer questions (SAQs) on this week’s lectures. They’re for practice, not to hand in.
instructions:
Optional practice. These short-answer questions go with this week’s lectures. Only the essay needs to be handed in, but SAQs are good practice at writing short, focused answers, and they’re good revision too.

  • Each is marked out of five, so answer in bullet points and aim for at least five separate points.
  • There’s no time limit, but about 10 minutes for each is a good aim.
  • For the loop in the first question, use Insert drawing (the pencil), or draw it on paper and add a photo of it with Insert picture.
  • Answer as many as you like. You can leave some blank and still submit.
  • After you submit, Review my answers shows you the points a good answer covers.

questions.title: A pressure–volume loop
questions.text:
A left ventricle has an EDV of 120 mL and an ESV of 50 mL. Sketch and label its pressure–volume loop. Identify the four valve events and the phases during which both valves are closed. Calculate stroke volume and indicate when S1 and S2 occur.

Draw the loop with Insert drawing (the pencil), or draw it on paper and add a photo of it with Insert picture.
questions.guidance:
• The loop. Plot left ventricular pressure (up) against volume (across). The loop runs anticlockwise: filling along the bottom, from the end-systolic volume (50 mL) to the end-diastolic volume (120 mL), at low pressure; isovolumetric contraction straight up the right-hand side; ejection across the top, back to 50 mL; and isovolumetric relaxation straight down the left-hand side.
  • The four valve events. The mitral valve closes at the bottom right corner, when ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure (end-diastolic volume). The aortic valve opens at the top right, when ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure (about 80 mmHg). The aortic valve closes at the top left, when ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure at the end of ejection (end-systolic volume). The mitral valve opens at the bottom left, when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, and filling begins.
  • Both valves closed. During isovolumetric contraction and isovolumetric relaxation, the two vertical sides. With both valves shut, no blood can enter or leave, so the volume stays the same while the pressure changes.
  • Stroke volume = EDV − ESV = 120 − 50 = 70 mL, the width of the loop. (The ejection fraction is 70/120, about 58%, and at 70 beats a minute the cardiac output would be about 4.9 L a minute.)
  • S1 and S2. S1 comes as the mitral (and tricuspid) valves close, at the start of isovolumetric contraction. S2 comes as the aortic (and pulmonary) valves close, at the start of isovolumetric relaxation.
  • For more marks. The area inside the loop is the stroke work, the external work the ventricle does in one beat. In aortic stenosis the ventricle has to generate a higher pressure to eject, so the top of the loop rises, and with a higher afterload the end-systolic volume tends to rise and the stroke volume to fall.

questions.title: Water between plasma and interstitial fluid
questions.text: What factors influence water movement between plasma and interstitial fluid?
questions.guidance:
• Use the Starling equation as the frame. Water moves across the capillary wall by convection, through and between the endothelial cells, driven by the balance of hydrostatic and colloid osmotic pressures: JV = Kf[(Pc − Pif) − σ(πc − πg)]. Take each term in turn: what it means, what it does, and why it might change.
  • Kf, the filtration coefficient, is the surface area times the hydraulic conductivity of the wall. It’s low in the tight capillaries of the brain and very high in the fenestrated capillaries of the renal glomeruli.
  • The hydrostatic pressures. Capillary pressure, Pc, follows venous pressure more closely than arterial pressure, because the resistance before the capillaries is much higher than the resistance after them. So it rises in heart failure, or in the legs when you stand still for a long time, and filtration rises. Interstitial pressure, Pif, is slightly negative in most tissues and opposes filtration when it rises, which is why compression stockings help.
  • The colloid osmotic pressures. Only solutes that can’t easily cross the wall exert an effective osmotic pressure, so Na+, which crosses freely, contributes almost nothing, though plasma has about 100 times as much of it as protein. The plasma proteins, mainly albumin, give about 25 mmHg. It falls in malnutrition, liver disease and the nephrotic syndrome. In the glycocalyx model, what matters is the difference between the plasma and the protein-poor space just under the glycocalyx (πg), which predicts a small net filtration along most capillaries rather than filtration followed by reabsorption.
  • σ, the reflection coefficient. From 1 (protein can’t cross) to 0 (it crosses freely). Inflammatory mediators such as histamine make capillaries leakier, so σ falls and fluid leaves.
  • The lymphatics. The small net filtration, 2 to 4 litres a day with 100 to 200 g of protein, is returned to the blood by the lymphatics. Oedema develops when filtration exceeds lymphatic return. When capillary pressure falls after a haemorrhage, the balance reverses and fluid moves into the blood (autotransfusion), though only for a while.

questions.title: The endothelium and vasodilatation
questions.text: Explain how the endothelium can cause vasodilatation of arterioles.
questions.guidance:
• The signal. Agonists such as acetylcholine and bradykinin act on receptors on the endothelial cells, raising their Ca2+. Ca2+–calmodulin activates nitric oxide synthase, which makes nitric oxide (NO) from L-arginine. The shear stress of flowing blood stimulates NO production too.
  • Paracrine action. NO is a small, lipophilic gas, so it diffuses straight from the endothelium into the smooth muscle around it.
  • In the smooth muscle. NO stimulates a soluble guanylyl cyclase, which makes cGMP. cGMP activates protein kinase G, which relaxes the muscle in two ways: it lowers the [Ca2+]i, and it lowers the sensitivity of the contractile machinery to Ca2+, chiefly by increasing the activity of myosin light-chain phosphatase. Less myosin is phosphorylated, the cross-bridges cycle less, tension falls, and the arteriole dilates.
  • The evidence. Furchgott found that acetylcholine relaxed arteries only when their endothelium was intact; rubbed off, they no longer relaxed, though they still contracted to noradrenaline. The relaxing factor was later shown to be NO (the Nobel Prize of 1998).
  • Drugs. Nitrates such as glyceryl trinitrate release NO and have relieved angina for over a century; sildenafil inhibits the phosphodiesterase (PDE5) that breaks down cGMP.
  • For more marks. The endothelium releases other dilators too, such as prostacyclin, as well as constrictors, and its net effect is normally to dilate. Endothelial dysfunction, as in hypertension, diabetes, obesity and smoking, loses this dilatation, and raises vascular resistance and the risk of atherosclerosis and clots.
